key_concept: At ovulation the released cell is a secondary oocyte (commonly called the ovum), and its own non-cellular glycoprotein envelope is the zona pellucida, with corona radiata follicle cells outside it.
steps: In a Graafian follicle, the secondary oocyte is enclosed by a non-cellular glycoprotein layer called the zona pellucida.
Outside the zona pellucida lie layers of follicle (granulosa) cells, which form the corona radiata.
At ovulation (around day 14), the Graafian follicle ruptures and the secondary oocyte is released, arrested at metaphase II.
It leaves still surrounded by the zona pellucida, with the corona radiata outside it.
Endometrium is the uterine lining and chorion is an extra-embryonic membrane, so neither covers the ovum.
Among the given options, only zona pellucida is the covering of the ovum, so option (3) is correct.
why_not_others: Zona radiata is a distractor built by mixing up 'zona pellucida' and 'corona radiata'; the term is used for the egg envelope in some non-mammalian vertebrates such as fish, not in standard human terminology. Endometrium is the inner lining of the uterus, and chorion forms after fertilisation as a foetal membrane that contributes to the placenta.
common_trap: Students blend 'corona radiata' and 'zona pellucida' into 'zona radiata', or pick chorion because it is also a membrane linked to pregnancy.
time_saving_tip: Remember the human pair: zona pellucida is the inner, non-cellular layer and corona radiata is the outer, cellular layer. Any option outside this pair, except zona pellucida itself, can be eliminated.
